lines.raw: "How many members do we have?" is a tricky question.
lines.say: "How many members do we have?" is a tricky question.

scenes.section: "How many members do we have?" is a tricky question

lines.raw: Members join and leave every month.
lines.say: Members join and leave every month.

lines.raw: If a plan had 1,000 members in January and 1,500 in December, how many members did it have "in 2025"?
lines.say: If a plan had 1,000 members in January and 1,500 in December, how many members did it have "in 2025"?

lines.raw: Neither number is fair.
lines.say: Neither number is fair.

lines.raw: So insurers count **member months** instead.
lines.say: So insurers count member months instead.

scenes.section: "How many members do we have?" is a tricky question

lines.raw: Think of renting a flat.
lines.say: Think of renting a flat.

lines.raw: A landlord in Kathmandu with one flat rented for 12 months, and another rented for only 6, has had **18 flat-months** of rent this year.
lines.say: A landlord in Kathmandu with one flat rented for 12 months, and another rented for only 6, has had 18 flat-months of rent this year.

lines.raw: Counting "2 flats" would hide that one stood empty for half the year.
lines.say: Counting "2 flats" would hide that one stood empty for half the year.

lines.raw: A **member month** is the same idea: **one person covered for one month**.
lines.say: A member month is the same idea: one person covered for one month.

scenes.section: "How many members do we have?" is a tricky question

lines.raw: Member months.
lines.say: Member months.

lines.raw: Member months equals sum of (months each member was covered).
lines.say: Member months equals sum of (months each member was covered).

lines.raw: For example: Emily's family in 2025: Emily 12 plus Lily 12 plus Daniel 6 (July to December) equals 30 member months.
lines.say: For example: Emily's family in 2025: Emily 12 plus Lily 12 plus Daniel 6 (July to December) equals 30 member months.

scenes.section: "How many members do we have?" is a tricky question

lines.raw: From member months to average members.
lines.say: From member months to average members.

lines.raw: Divide member months by 12 to get the **average number of members** in the year.
lines.say: Divide member months by 12 to get the average number of members in the year.

lines.raw: Emily's family: 30 ÷ 12 = **2.5** average members.
lines.say: Emily's family: 30 ÷ 12 = 2.5 average members.

lines.raw: That is fair: two people all year plus one person for half the year.
lines.say: That is fair: two people all year plus one person for half the year.

lines.raw: Counting months from spans.
lines.say: Counting months from spans.

lines.raw: Most US spans start on the **1st** of a month and end on the **last day** of a month.
lines.say: Most U S spans start on the 1st of a month and end on the last day of a month.

lines.raw: Then counting is easy: count every month the span touches inside your reporting period.
lines.say: Then counting is easy: count every month the span touches inside your reporting period.

lines.raw: Months in a whole-month span (after cutting it to the reporting period).
lines.say: Months in a whole-month span (after cutting it to the reporting period).

lines.raw: Months equals (end year − start year) times 12 plus (end month − start month) plus 1.
lines.say: Months equals (end year − start year) times 12 plus (end month − start month) plus 1.

lines.raw: For example: Daniel: 2025-07-01 to 9999-12-31.
lines.say: For example: Daniel: 2025-07-01 to 9999-12-31.

lines.raw: Months equals 0 times 12 plus (12 − 7) plus 1 equals 6.
lines.say: Months equals 0 times 12 plus (12 − 7) plus 1 equals 6.

lines.raw: Always cut spans to the reporting period first.
lines.say: Always cut spans to the reporting period first.

lines.raw: Emily's span starts in **2022** and has no end (`9999-12-31`).
lines.say: Emily's span starts in 2022 and has no end (9 9 9 9 dash 1 2 dash 3 1).

lines.raw: If you forget to cut it to 2025, you will count thousands of months.
lines.say: If you forget to cut it to 2025, you will count thousands of months.

lines.raw: For a 2025 report, every span is clipped to **2025-01-01 to 2025-12-31** before counting.
lines.say: For a 2025 report, every span is clipped to 2025-01-01 to 2025-12-31 before counting.

lines.raw: What about mid-month dates?
lines.say: What about mid-month dates?

lines.raw: Some spans start or end in the middle of a month.
lines.say: Some spans start or end in the middle of a month.

lines.raw: Does that month count?
lines.say: Does that month count?

lines.raw: There is **no single national rule**.
lines.say: There is no single national rule.

lines.raw: Each organisation picks a convention and uses it consistently.
lines.say: Each organisation picks a convention and uses it consistently.

lines.raw: Three common ones:
lines.say: Three common ones:

lines.raw: Here is a quick table.
lines.say: Here is a quick table.

lines.raw: **1st-of-month rule**. A month counts if the member was covered...: ...on the **1st** of that month.
lines.say: 1st-of-month rule. A month counts if the member was covered...: ...on the 1st of that month.

lines.raw: **Any-day rule**. A month counts if the member was covered...: ...on **at least one day** of that month.
lines.say: Any-day rule. A month counts if the member was covered...: ...on at least one day of that month.

lines.raw: **15th rule (mid-month)**. A month counts if the member was covered...: ...on the **15th** of that month.
lines.say: 15th rule (mid-month). A month counts if the member was covered...: ...on the 15th of that month.

lines.raw: Four members, January to March 2025 (Q1), counted three ways.
lines.say: Four members, January to March 2025 (Q1), counted three ways.

lines.raw: Same people, three answers.
lines.say: Same people, three answers.

lines.raw: The same four people give **6, 8 or 7** member months.
lines.say: The same four people give 6, 8 or 7 member months.

lines.raw: None is wrong; they are just different rules.
lines.say: None is wrong; they are just different rules.

lines.raw: When you compare numbers from two reports, first check they use the **same convention**.
lines.say: When you compare numbers from two reports, first check they use the same convention.

lines.raw: Some teams avoid the problem by counting **days** instead (e.g. 17 days in a 31-day month = 0.55 of a month).
lines.say: Some teams avoid the problem by counting days instead (for example 17 days in a 31-day month = 0.55 of a month).

lines.raw: PMPM: cost per member per month.
lines.say: P M P M: cost per member per month.

scenes.section: PMPM: cost per member per month

lines.raw: Once you have member months, you can compare costs fairly.
lines.say: Once you have member months, you can compare costs fairly.

lines.raw: The standard measure is **PMPM**: per member per month.
lines.say: The standard measure is P M P M: per member per month.

scenes.section: PMPM: cost per member per month

lines.raw: PMPM.
lines.say: P M P M.

lines.raw: PMPM equals Total cost ÷ Member months.
lines.say: P M P M equals Total cost ÷ Member months.

lines.raw: For example: "Total cost" is usually the sum of paid amounts (paid PMPM) or allowed amounts (allowed PMPM).
lines.say: For example: "Total cost" is usually the sum of paid amounts (paid P M P M) or allowed amounts (allowed P M P M).

scenes.section: Worked example: why "per member" is not enough

lines.raw: Here is a quick table.
lines.say: Here is a quick table.

lines.raw: Members. Plan A: 1,000, all year. Plan B: 750 all year + 750 who joined on 1 July.
lines.say: Members. Plan A: 1,000, all year. Plan B: 750 all year and 750 who joined on 1 July.

lines.raw: Members at year end. Plan A: 1,000. Plan B: 1,500.
lines.say: Members at year end. Plan A: 1,000. Plan B: 1,500.

lines.raw: Total paid in the year. Plan A: $6,000,000. Plan B: $6,075,000.
lines.say: Total paid in the year. Plan A: 6000000 dollars. Plan B: 6075000 dollars.

lines.raw: Cost per year-end member (misleading). Plan A: $6,000,000 ÷ 1,000 = $6,000. Plan B: $6,075,000 ÷ 1,500 = $4,050.
lines.say: Cost per year-end member (misleading). Plan A: 6000000 dollars ÷ 1,000 = 6000 dollars. Plan B: 6075000 dollars ÷ 1,500 = 4050 dollars.
P M P M (fair). Plan A: 6000000 dollars ÷ 12,000 = 500 dollars. Plan B: 6075000 dollars ÷ 13,500 = 450 dollars.

scenes.section: Worked example: why "per member" is not enough

lines.raw: What changed?
lines.say: What changed?

lines.raw: Divided by year-end members, Plan B looks about **a third cheaper** ($4,050 vs $6,000).
lines.say: Divided by year-end members, Plan B looks about a third cheaper (4050 dollars versus 6000 dollars).

lines.raw: But half its members were only there for 6 months.
lines.say: But half its members were only there for 6 months.

lines.raw: PMPM shows the fair difference: **$450 vs $500**, about 10% cheaper.
lines.say: P M P M shows the fair difference: 450 dollars versus 500 dollars about 10 percent cheaper.

lines.raw: PMPY (per member per year).
lines.say: P M P Y (per member per year).

Plan A: 500 dollars × 12 = 6000 dollars P M P Y.

lines.raw: Premium PMPM.
lines.say: Premium P M P M.

lines.raw: The premium the insurer collects per member per month.
lines.say: The premium the insurer collects per member per month.

lines.raw: Comparing it with cost PMPM shows whether a plan makes or loses money.
lines.say: Comparing it with cost P M P M shows whether a plan makes or loses money.

lines.raw: Medical loss ratio (MLR).
lines.say: Medical loss ratio (M L R).

lines.raw: Claims cost ÷ premium.
lines.say: Claims cost ÷ premium.

lines.raw: The ACA requires insurers to spend at least **80%** (individual and small group) or **85%** (large group) of premiums on care and quality, or refund the difference.
lines.say: The A C A requires insurers to spend at least 80 percent (individual and small group) or 85 percent (large group) of premiums on care and quality, or refund the difference.

lines.raw: Utilisation per 1,000.
lines.say: Utilisation per 1,000.

lines.raw: Events (visits, admissions) ÷ member months × 12,000.
lines.say: Events (visits, admissions) ÷ member months × 12,000.

lines.raw: A fair way to compare how often members use care.
lines.say: A fair way to compare how often members use care.
